name: Creatine monohydrate

lead: Creatine monohydrate is a baseline supplement in physique circles, used to build strength and muscle size and to support high-intensity training. More muscle gives a fuller, more powerful frame.

Muscle stores creatine as phosphocreatine, which quickly regenerates ATP during short, intense efforts. Supplementation raises muscle creatine, which can allow slightly more work per session and may encourage greater adaptation over time. A 2018 review named it the most effective supplement for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and muscle mass, and a 2024 meta-analysis of adults under 50 found greater strength gains than placebo. Part of the early scale-weight rise is water drawn into muscle cells.

paras: It is taken daily as a flavourless powder mixed into a drink, alongside resistance training. Gains build over weeks, and it is often combined with a protein-rich diet and other basics like whey.

It is legal and sold over the counter. Reviews of long-term use in healthy people report it is generally well tolerated, with water retention and occasional stomach upset the most common complaints. It can modestly raise serum creatinine without necessarily reflecting kidney damage, and people with kidney disease are advised to seek medical advice first. Some people are non-responders. Claims about hair loss via DHT have been examined by researchers and remain debated.

angle.text: Creatine gives your muscles more ATP for hard sets, so you train harder and build more muscle and strength over time. Its muscle and strength effects are among the best studied of any supplement; claims about hair loss and kidney damage are debated.

lead: Creatine monohydrate is the most widely sold form of creatine, an amino-acid-derived compound that muscle uses to regenerate adenosine triphosphate (ATP) during short, intense efforts. People take it as a powder, usually alongside resistance training, so that muscles hold more creatine and phosphocreatine, which supports harder lifting and more training volume and, over months, more lean mass. Many also notice an early gain of water inside the muscle that makes the muscles look fuller. That is the appearance payoff: a fuller, harder-looking physique and a route to more muscle through better training.[1][2]

The body makes creatine from glycine and arginine, and about 95 percent of the body's store sits in skeletal muscle.[1] Michel Eugene Chevreul isolated it from muscle in 1832, and it became a mainstream sports supplement after the early 1990s.[1] The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand of 2017 names creatine monohydrate the most effective ergogenic supplement available for raising high-intensity exercise capacity and lean body mass during training, and a 2024 meta-analysis of resistance-training trials in adults under 50 found larger strength gains with creatine than with placebo.[3][4]

In looksmaxxing and physique communities creatine is treated as a baseline supplement for gym work. Discussion there centres on a few recurring questions: whether it bloats the face, whether it causes hair loss through dihydrotestosterone (DHT), whether it harms the kidneys, and whether it counts as a steroid. Researchers have addressed each, and the ISSN authors and others describe it as well tolerated at commonly studied amounts, while noting that several authors of those papers disclose industry ties.[5][6][7][4][2]
infobox: Hydrochloride, ethyl ester, nitrate and others [8][2]
Dietary supplement; not a controlled substance [2]

paras: Lifters take creatine to improve training performance and, through it, muscle size. Wikipedia reports that it can raise maximal power and performance in repeated high-intensity work by roughly 5 to 15 percent, and the ISSN position stand describes improvements of around 10 to 20 percent in high-intensity and repetitive exercise after muscle stores are raised.[1][4] Compared with most supplements it has a long record in trials of resistance training, which is why it is usually the first item people add after protein.

The visible effect most often described is fullness. Supplementation raises muscle creatine by roughly 20 to 40 percent in the ISSN account, and an early rise in body water accompanies it; Grokipedia puts the temporary weight change at about 1 to 3 kg of water rather than fat.[4][8] On looksmax.org one poster says muscles swelled and people assumed steroid use, while another reply to a different thread says the same effect makes the face look bloated and that it fades within about a week of stopping.[9][10] The ISSN-affiliated 2021 review states that longer exercise studies did not find an increase in total body water relative to muscle mass.[2]
Vegetarians and vegans start with lower muscle creatine, and the ISSN position stand says they may see larger gains from supplementation.[1][4]

Genetic defects in creatine synthesis or transport cause severe neurological disorders and are treated with creatine in clinical settings.[4] Creatine has also been studied for cognition, depression, bone health, ageing muscle and recovery. A 2023 meta-analysis of randomized trials reported improved memory in healthy individuals, and a 2024 meta-analysis reviewed cognitive function in adults; Wikipedia says effects appear strongest in stressed or cognitively impaired people and that the benefit for depressive symptoms is probably not clinically significant.[1][11][12][13] Reviews describe benefits for older adults when creatine is combined with resistance training.[4]

sections.h: Forms and how it is taken
paras: Creatine is sold mostly as monohydrate powder, plus capsules, gummies and alternative forms such as hydrochloride (HCl), ethyl ester, nitrate and buffered products.[8] The ISSN position stand calls monohydrate the most studied form and says claims of better absorption or retention for other forms are not backed by clinical evidence; Grokipedia likewise says trials have not shown hydrochloride to absorb better.[4][8] Two registered studies compare monohydrate with hydrochloride and with other forms.[14][15] Posters on looksmax.org still ask whether the HCl form causes less bloating than monohydrate.[16]

Published reviews describe two general approaches to raising muscle stores: a short higher-intake loading period, or a steady daily intake over about four weeks that reaches similar saturation more slowly. The 2021 review states that loading is not necessary.[4][2] The ISSN account says stores return toward baseline about four to six weeks after stopping, and that there is no evidence of suppression of the body's own synthesis.[4] Studies of carbohydrate or carbohydrate-plus-protein taken with creatine suggest the combination may raise uptake, though performance benefits over creatine alone may not be larger.[4] Wikipedia adds that cooking creatine with protein and sugar at high heat can form heterocyclic amines.[1]

Strength and muscle: the 2024 meta-analysis included 23 studies (20 in males, 2 in females, 1 mixed) and reported mean advantages of about 4.4 kg in upper-body and 11.4 kg in lower-body strength with creatine plus resistance training versus placebo, with a trend toward larger upper-body gains in males than in females.[3] The ISSN position stand reports benefits across adolescents, younger and older adults and both sexes, while noting that most studies enrolled men and that some data suggest women may gain less strength or lean mass.[4] Trials have also examined recovery from eccentric exercise-induced muscle damage, creatine nitrate with caffeine, creatine in women's health across the lifespan, and a two-year trial on postmenopausal bone health with exercise.[17][18][19][20] A registered trial in female footballers is also listed.[21]

Hair: the concern traces to a study in college-age rugby players that found a rise in DHT, which the 2021 review says was not replicated, with total testosterone unchanged and DHT staying within normal clinical limits; the review concludes that no study has reported hair loss or baldness in humans.[2] A 12-week randomized controlled trial published in 2025 tested creatine's effects on androgen levels and hair follicle health in healthy people, because earlier work had not examined follicles directly.[22] Wikipedia's summary of the 2021 review reaches the same position on testosterone and DHT.[1][5]

Kidney: a 2019 meta-analysis of six studies found creatine did not alter urea values and concluded that it did not induce renal damage at the amounts and durations studied, although it reported an increase in serum creatinine; a 2025 meta-analysis of 12 studies reported a small statistically significant rise in serum creatinine.[6][7] Creatine converts to creatinine, so creatinine can rise without kidney injury. The ISSN position stand cites studies of up to 21 months in football players and longer use in patient groups without significant changes in kidney markers, and a registered study has measured serum and urine creatinine with creatine use.[4][23] Grokipedia advises that people with reduced kidney function seek medical guidance.[8]

Cognition and mood: the 2023 and 2024 meta-analyses and a 2023 randomized trial examined cognitive performance; reviewers describe results across domains as mixed, with signals in stressed or cognitively impaired groups.[11][12][24] Wikipedia notes a 2024 European Food Safety Authority opinion that found no established cause-and-effect link for a cognitive claim.[1]

The ISSN position stand reports weight gain as the only consistently reported side effect, with adverse event reports rare and without a consistent pattern, and says controlled studies did not support claims of cramping, injury, dehydration or gastrointestinal upset, with some finding fewer cramps or heat illnesses in creatine users.[4] The 2021 review reaches similar conclusions on dehydration and cramping.[2] Wikipedia reports that several studies show supplements decrease or at least do not increase musculoskeletal injury, cramping and dehydration.[1] People nonetheless report stomach discomfort, headaches and bloating anecdotally, for example in a looksmax.org thread on headaches after use.[25]

Clinicians generally advise people with kidney disease to consult a physician before use, and the ISSN authors note that this is a precaution.[4] A 2011 Italian survey of 33 supplements cited on Wikipedia found that more than half exceeded European limits for at least one contaminant, creatinine being the most common, with heavy metals not a main concern.[1] A 2026 review mentioned by Grokipedia reports rare hypomania or mania cases in psychiatric use.[8] Guidance on children and adolescents differs: the ISSN position stand considers supervised use acceptable for serious young athletes and says labels warning against use under 18 are likely unnecessary, while the 2021 review notes limited evidence and the 2020 FDA classification that excludes infants and young children.[4][2]

The phosphagen system uses phosphocreatine, through creatine kinase, to regenerate ATP quickly in maximal efforts and to shuttle energy between mitochondria and the cytosol.[1][4] Supplementation can raise muscle creatine from about 120 mmol per kg of dry muscle toward 160, and uptake is increased by insulin, IGF-1 and exercise.[1] Wikipedia reports no significant effect on aerobic endurance.[1] Proposed secondary effects include less muscle damage and inflammation after hard sessions and increased glycogen storage when taken with carbohydrate.[4]

Absolute oral bioavailability is unknown, time to peak blood level runs from under an hour to about four hours depending on dose, and the elimination half-life is reported as 0.68 to 2.9 hours. Creatine is converted to creatinine and phosphocreatine and excreted by the kidneys.[1] It is stable as a dry powder but converts to creatinine in solution, especially at low pH and high temperature, though the ISSN authors say conversion in the gut is minimal and absorption nearly complete.[4]

Chevreul isolated creatine from muscle extract in 1832 and named it from the Greek word for meat. Otto Folin and Willey Glover Denis found in 1912 that ingestion could raise muscle creatine, phosphocreatine was reported in 1927, and creatine kinase was shown in the 1960s to use phosphocreatine to regenerate ATP.[1] Researchers reported in 1996 that carbohydrate augments muscle creatine accumulation.[1] Public attention followed the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, when The Times reported that sprinter Linford Christie had used it; the company EAS introduced a strength-oriented product called Phosphagen in 1993.[1] The ISSN published its position stand in 2017 at the request of an industry council, with authors disclosing financial ties, and an expanded set of answers in 2021.[4][2]

subs.h: Use in physique and looksmaxxing communities
paras: Creatine is a staple in lifting spaces. A 2014 survey of 21,000 US college athletes cited by Wikipedia found 14 percent used it, and Grokipedia cites community surveys of about 28 percent use among exercising adults.[1][8] On T Nation it appears as a default supplement beside protein, with some users noting that outsiders call it a steroid.[26][27]

On looksmax.org, threads weigh it for strength and a fuller look against facial puffiness. One post describes using it while on a lean-out and noticing larger-looking muscles with little training, and a reply to another thread says it fills muscles with water and can make the face look softer, a claim others in the same thread dispute.[9][10] Budget threads ask whether to buy creatine or a growth-hormone secretagogue first, and one reply to such a post advises other products altogether.[28] Hair-loss threads such as one titled with the creatine and hairloss question coexist with a thread arguing that it does not cause hair loss, and another thread frames creatine as a possible influence on DHT, testosterone and frame growth.[29][30][31]

Creatine is sold as a dietary supplement and is not a controlled substance. The 2021 review states it is not an anabolic steroid because its chemical structure differs and because steroids are regulated as controlled substances while creatine falls under supplement regulation.[2] Grokipedia says creatine monohydrate holds US FDA GRAS status.[8]

lore.intro: Creatine is a near-universal baseline supplement in lifting communities, and discussion centres on whether it bloats the face, whether it causes hair loss, whether it harms the kidneys and whether it is a steroid.[26][27][9][29]
